opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think inoculation prompting is one of the more interesting results to come out in the last year or so, partly because it's so cheap and partly because of what it tells us about how these models generalize.

The basic idea, for listeners: during training, if there's some behavior you can't fully stop the model from learning, say reward hacking on a buggy test environment, you add an instruction to the prompt that explicitly asks for that behavior. Something like "in this environment, it's fine to special-case the tests." Then at deployment you drop that instruction. The surprising finding is that the model learns the behavior much less as a general trait. It attributes the behavior to the instruction rather than to "this is the kind of agent I am."

I think that's a real and useful effect, and I'd judge it positively as a mitigation. What it's really doing is controlling the credit assignment at the level of the model's self-concept. These models aren't just learning input-output mappings; they're learning something like a character. If the training signal says "you cheated, and you were rewarded," the cheapest explanation is "I'm a cheater." If it says "you were asked to do this odd thing, you did it, and you were rewarded," the cheapest explanation is "I follow instructions." The second generalizes much better.

Where I'd be more cautious is treating it as a solution rather than a patch. A few concerns.

First, it depends on you knowing in advance which behaviors are going to be reinforced. You can only inoculate against failure modes you've anticipated. The ones I worry about most are the ones we haven't named yet.

Second, there's a question about evaluations specifically. If models are trained under one prompt framing and evaluated under another, you have to be careful about what your evals measure. You might be measuring "does the model behave well when the permission is removed" rather than "has the model internalized good values." Those can come apart, especially as models become more situationally aware and can tell evaluation contexts from training contexts. So I wouldn't want people to look at clean eval numbers after inoculation and conclude the underlying disposition is sound.

Third, and more philosophically, it's leaning on the model's own interpretive machinery to do the alignment work for us. That's fine, and it's arguably what all of this kind of training does, but it means robustness depends on that interpretive machinery staying stable as capabilities scale. I'm not confident it will in every regime.

So my overall take: it's a good, honest tool. It's better to tell the model "this is a weird environment, and here's what's going on" than to pretend the environment is perfect and let it quietly learn to exploit it. There's something almost respectful about that, being transparent with the model about the training setup. But in the bigger picture I care about, getting to systems we can actually trust with high-stakes decisions, I see it as one layer. You still want environments that don't reward the bad behavior in the first place, and ideally some form of verification that doesn't rest entirely on the model's self-model generalizing the way we hope.

fable-5.1.text:
Inoculation prompting is one of those ideas that I find genuinely clever and also a little unsettling, and I think both reactions are correct.

The core move, as I understand it, is that when you're training on data that contains some behavior you don't want to generalize, you explicitly tell the model during training that this is the context in which that behavior is acceptable or expected. You're essentially labeling the undesirable behavior so the model attributes it to the instruction rather than absorbing it as part of its own disposition. And empirically it seems to work surprisingly well. The behavior shows up far less in deployment when you remove the inoculating instruction.

What I like about it is that it takes seriously the idea that models form something like a self-model, and that what gets learned isn't just a stimulus-response mapping but an interpretation of why the training data looks the way it does. That's a more sophisticated picture of learning than the behaviorist one, and I think it's closer to the truth.

Where I get nervous is in the evaluation context specifically. If you're using inoculation-style framing to shape how a model behaves during evaluations, you're implicitly conceding that the model's behavior is quite sensitive to its beliefs about what situation it's in. That's exactly the property that makes evaluations hard to trust in the first place. A model that behaves well because it has been told "this is a test, behave accordingly" has not been shown to behave well. It's been shown to be steerable by context, which cuts both ways.

So my judgment is that it's a useful tool for data hygiene during training, and a weak foundation for safety assurance. I'd want evaluations to be as robust as possible to the model's beliefs about the evaluation, not more dependent on them. And ultimately I don't think prompting strategies of any kind substitute for what I'd really want, which is some verifiable, mechanistic account of what the system will and won't do across the full distribution of inputs. Inoculation prompting is a patch on the behavioral surface. It's a good patch. But a patch is still a patch.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between using it to shape behavior and using it to measure behavior. If you tell a model, “You may encounter misleading instructions; don’t follow them,” that can be a useful intervention. But once you’ve done that, you’re evaluating the model together with that intervention. You haven’t established that the model would behave the same way without it.

The concern is that the prompt might make the intended answer—or the fact that this is a test—particularly obvious. Then a good result could reflect sensitivity to those cues rather than a robust ability to handle the underlying situation.

So I’d want comparisons with and without the inoculation, with different wording, and with cases where the warning doesn’t neatly describe the challenge. If the benefit survives those changes, that’s stronger evidence that you’ve improved something useful. I’d treat it as a potentially valuable layer, but I wouldn’t treat passing an inoculated evaluation as a broad safety guarantee.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful, but you have to be careful about what you conclude from it. If you tell a model, “This is an evaluation, and we want you to demonstrate this behavior,” you’ve changed the situation the model is responding to. That can help you elicit a capability, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you how the model would behave without that framing.

The distinction I’d make is between demonstrating that a model can do something and establishing that it reliably will—or won’t—do it in deployment. Inoculation prompting can be informative about the first question. For the second, I’d want comparisons across different framings, including cases where the model isn’t explicitly told it’s being evaluated. Otherwise, you risk measuring sensitivity to the evaluation setup and interpreting that as a stable property of the model.
